checkpoints.title: Tradeoff duel
checkpoints.prompt: 5M points/sec of time-series. What stores them?

options.label: Relational table
options.verdict: Every point is a row and every index is rewritten on insert. Worse, the query you actually run — one metric across a time range — scatters across the whole table because rows are laid out by arrival, not by series.

options.label: Time-series store
options.verdict: Points for one series land together and compress hard, because adjacent timestamps and near-identical values delta-encode to almost nothing. Retention becomes dropping a partition instead of a mass DELETE.

defend.prompt: What does the time-series engine buy you specifically?

options.label: Range scans on one series stay contiguous on disk
Retention is a partition drop, not a delete storm
Delta and dictionary encoding shrink storage by an order of magnitude
Arbitrary joins across metrics get faster

defend.explain: Joins are exactly what these engines give up. You trade relational flexibility for write throughput, compression and cheap expiry — which is the right trade when the query is always 'this series, this window'.

checkpoints.title: Capacity ladder
checkpoints.prompt: 500K hosts, 100 metrics each, emitted every 10 seconds.

rungs.note: Before compression — which is why compression is not optional here.
Which is why raw is downsampled into rollups rather than kept.

checkpoints.explain: 5M points/sec is survivable; 1.3 PB of raw is not, at least not at full resolution. Retention policy is a storage design decision, not an afterthought.

checkpoints.title: Architecture builder
checkpoints.prompt: Build the ingest path from an agent to a queryable point.
checkpoints.explain: Kafka absorbs the burst and decouples agents from storage, so a slow write never backs up into the fleet. The stream processor does downsampling and rollups on the way in. The alert engine and dashboards read from the TSDB — they are consumers, not part of ingest.

checkpoints.title: Spot the bottleneck
checkpoints.prompt: Alerts are firing 8 minutes late. Dashboards look fine for older data.
checkpoints.explain: Both alerting and storage read from the same stream, and the stream is 40M points behind. Old dashboards look fine because that data already landed; anything recent has not arrived yet. The alert engine is evaluating correctly against data that is simply not there. Scale consumers, or give alerting its own lower-latency path off the ingest topic.

wrong.Alert Engine: 400ms evaluation is not 8 minutes. It is judging stale input, not running slowly.
wrong.Time-series DB: Writes are fast — there just are not enough of them arriving.
wrong.Ingest Service: Agents are being accepted fine; the backlog is after ingest.
